topic.title: Geometric Clustering, Stability, and Coresets
topic.overview: Geometric clustering groups points around representative centers, often by minimizing distances as in k-means. This topic examines initialization, local search, approximation guarantees, compressed datasets called coresets, and sensitivity to missing or changing observations. A representative stability analysis measures how much an algorithm's output changes when a random input point is removed.
topic.whyItMatters: A low clustering objective does not guarantee that the result is stable or that a particular optimizer will find meaningful groups. Algorithmic guarantees clarify the effects of dimension, noise, initialization, and data reduction on practical conclusions.
topic.evolution: Early representatives study convergence and improved starting points. Later work adds stable instances, fairness, missing values, and dynamic updates. Recent analyses contrast Lloyd and Hartigan updates in high-dimensional noise, showing that algorithms targeting the same objective can behave very differently.
openQuestions: Which stability measures predict useful clusters in real applications?
Can compact coresets preserve fairness and robustness as well as the clustering objective?
